newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: IMF sees new growth in Colombia's fiscal deficit.
newsitem.headline: IMF sees new growth in Colombia's fiscal deficit.

text.p: BOGOTA, May 18 Reuter - The International Monetary Fund (IMF) forecast Colombia's central government fiscal deficit would grow to between 4.5 percent and 5.0 percent of gross domestic product GDP this year, the respected El Espectador newspaper said Sunday, citing a confidential report.
The critical report also predicts overall GDP growth will be about 3.2 percent, compared to the 4.0 percent the government is currently forecasting.

If its proves correct the IMF forecast will cause a fresh headache for President Ernesto Samper's government, which declared an economic state of emergency in January when it emerged the 1996 fiscal deficit hit more than 4.0 percent of GDP compared to just 0.2 percent of GDP in 1995.

The IMF, according to the El Espectador newspaper, is also skeptical of Finance Minister Jose Antonio Ocampo's growth rate forecast of 4.0 percent. The IMF predicts a 3.2 percent growth in GDP, up from 2.1 percent in 1996, one of the lowest rates in a decade.
IMF chief Michel Camdessus will personally deliver his report to Samper this week, according to El Espectador.

In it, the IMF is critical of what it sees as Colombia's bid to boost short term growth while sacrificing economic fundamentals such as reining in the fiscal deficit and taking steps to permanently peg back inflation.

"Colombia's economic policy lacks a broad perspective. It seems that the recovery of vigorous economic activity is the authorities' central objective, even above that of resolving deep-rooted fiscal problems and the definitve reduction of inflation," El Espectador quoted the IMF report as saying.
The IMF does, however, share the government's view that inflation will be cut to 18 percent this year, compared with 21.63 percent in 1996.
It also forecasts that the nominal devaluation of Colombia's peso currency will be 17 percent, two percentage points ahead of the government's minimum devaluation target of 15 percent.
Among the recommendations of the IMF report, El Espectador said, was that Colombia should "rapidly introduce" a system to review macroeconomic targets on a quarterly basis.

It delivered stinging criticism of the Samper administration for caving in to union pressures after a week-long strike in February and granting public sector wage hikes in excess of the 13.5 percent weighted increase first offered.
"Monetary policy has been relaxed and the heavy indebtedness of the public sector will continue weakening the private sector and undermine the balance of payments current account," the report said.
The IMF report obtained by El Espectador warns of the risk of a "serious weakening of the economy in 1998" if the combination of medium term and short term economic policies are not reviewed.

It advises: "Our advice is clear - avoid relaxed or cyclical policies and begin to get the fundmentals right in order to create the conditions for solid recovery, which could intially slow down the economy but will later translate into robust and sustainable growth."
